questions.q: Meera draws a cross-section for her project and labels only the crust as the 'lithosphere', saying, 'Plates are just the crust.' Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: The lithosphere is the crust plus the upper mantle, and this layer is broken into plates. The chapter says the crust along with the upper part of the mantle forms the lithosphere, and the lithosphere is what is broken into tectonic plates.
o: The lithosphere is the crust plus the upper mantle, and this layer is broken into plates
The lithosphere is the crust together with the outer core, and plates are cut from both of these layers
The lithosphere is the crust alone, so her label is right, but the plates lie in the layer beneath it
The lithosphere is the semi-molten layer beneath the crust, and plates are slabs cut from that layer

questions.q: Arjun fills a glass tank with water, puts a small flame under its middle and floats a cork on top. He sees the water rise at the middle, spread sideways and sink at the edges, and the cork is carried along. In the chapter's explanation of moving plates, which part of his set-up plays the role of the heat from the Earth's core?
questions.a: The flame under the middle of the tank. The flame is the heat source; in the Earth, heat from the core makes mantle material rise while cooler material sinks, and these convection currents push and pull the plates (the cork).
o: The flame under the middle of the tank
The cork carried along at the surface
The water sinking at the edges
The glass wall of the tank

questions.q: Four seismic survey sites report these crust thicknesses: 5 km, 7 km, 33 km and 6 km. Using the ranges the chapter gives, which reading could NOT come from crust under an ocean?
questions.a: 33 km. Oceanic crust is 5-7 km thick, while crust under continents is 30-40 km; only 33 km falls outside the oceanic range.
o: 33 km
7 km
6 km
5 km

questions.q: A student measures a plate that moves 4 cm every year. If the plate keeps the same speed, how far does it travel in 2.5 crore (25 million) years?
questions.a: About 1000 km. 4 cm x 25,000,000 years = 100,000,000 cm = 1000 km; so even a few cm a year adds up to a huge distance.
o: About 1000 km
About 100 km
About 10 km
About 10,000 km

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The lithosphere is not the same layer as the crust.
Reason (R): The crust is the outermost layer of the Earth, on which we live.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The lithosphere also contains the upper part of the mantle, so A is true. R is a true fact about the crust but it does not explain why the lithosphere is a bigger layer.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the layers of the Earth.
1. The inner core is a solid, hot, spinning metal ball and is the densest part of the Earth.
2. The outer core is a fluid layer made mainly of iron and nickel.
3. The lithosphere is made of the whole mantle together with the crust.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only. Statements 1 and 2 are from the chapter. Statement 3 is false: the lithosphere is the crust with only the upper part of the mantle, not the whole mantle.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Match each layer in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Asthenosphere  2. Outer core  3. Lithosphere  4. Inner core
Column II: (a) Solid, hot spinning metal ball, the densest part  (b) Fluid layer mainly of iron and nickel  (c) Rigid outer layer including the crust and upper mantle  (d) Hot, mobile layer of partially molten rock
questions.a: 1-d, 2-b, 3-c, 4-a. The asthenosphere is the partially molten mobile layer, the outer core is the fluid iron-nickel layer, the lithosphere is the rigid outer layer and the inner core is the solid, densest ball.

questions.q: A survey team finds that one plate carries the floor of a wide ocean and, along one edge, a whole continent as well. Which of the chapter's three types of tectonic plate is this?
questions.a: A mixed plate. A plate that carries both continents and ocean floors is a mixed plate; 'convergent' names a boundary type, not a plate type.
o: A mixed plate
A continental plate
An oceanic plate
A convergent plate

questions.q: True or False: Because tectonic plates are massive slabs of solid rock, they must be sliding over another layer of solid rock.
questions.a: False. The plates move over the asthenosphere, which is semi-molten and allows them to move.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the layer beneath the lithosphere is the semi-molten asthenosphere

questions.q: (a) What is the thickness of the crust under continents, according to the chapter? (b) Using the thickest continental figure and the thinnest ocean figure, how many times thicker is the continental crust?
questions.a: (a) 30-40 km. (b) 40 km / 5 km = 8 times thicker (the ratio runs from about 4.3 times, 30/7, to 8 times, 40/5, across the ranges).
s: (a) 30-40 km under continents
(b) 40 / 5 = 8 times, worked from the chapter's ranges

questions.q: Differentiate between the lithosphere and the asthenosphere on two points: what each is made of and what each does when the plates move.
questions.a: The lithosphere is rigid (crust plus upper mantle) and is broken into the tectonic plates that move. The asthenosphere lies beneath it, is semi-molten and mobile, and allows the plates to move.
s: Lithosphere: rigid, crust with upper mantle, broken into plates
Asthenosphere: semi-molten layer beneath that allows the plates to move

questions.q: (a) Which material in the mantle rises, and which sinks, according to the chapter? (b) Explain how this continuous movement makes a tectonic plate move.
questions.a: (a) Heated material (from the Earth's core) rises, while cooler material sinks. (b) This continuous rising and sinking sets up convection currents that push and pull the plates, moving them in different directions.
s: (a) Heated material rises; cooler material sinks
(b) The convection currents push and pull the plates

questions.q: Sneha says, 'A continental plate carries only land.' Correct her using the chapter's three plate types, giving one example of a plate that proves her wrong.
questions.a: She is wrong. A continental plate carries continents, an oceanic plate carries ocean floors, and a mixed plate carries both continents and oceans, so a mixed plate (such as one carrying a continent and part of an ocean) shows that plates do not carry only land.
s: States the three plate types correctly
Names the mixed plate as the counter-example

questions.q: Rahul says, 'The Earth has a crust, a mantle and a core, and all of it is hot, soft, semi-molten rock; that is why plates can float on it.' How far is he right?
questions.a: Partly right. He is right that the Earth has crust, mantle and core and that the mantle is hot. He is wrong that all of it is semi-molten: the inner core is solid, the outer core is fluid, and it is only the asthenosphere that is the semi-molten layer on which plates move.
s: Verdict: partly right
The right half: three layers and a hot mantle
The wrong half: only the asthenosphere is semi-molten; the inner core is solid

questions.q: Describe a kitchen or classroom activity that models how convection currents move a plate. Name what stands for the Earth's core heat, the rising material, the sinking material and the plate.
questions.a: Any valid model, e.g. a pan of water with coloured drops heated from below and a piece of paper floating on top: the burner stands for heat from the core, water rising in the middle for the rising mantle material, water sinking at the edges for the cooler sinking material, and the floating paper for the plate that is pushed and pulled along.
s: A believable set-up with a heat source
Rising and sinking material correctly named
The floating piece shown to be pushed and pulled like a plate

questions.q: A model of the Earth uses 1 cm for every 1000 km. Using the chapter's approximate values, find the length in cm that stands for each of the mantle (2900 km), the outer core (2200 km), the inner core (1250 km) and the lithosphere (100 km). Would the 30 km continental crust be easy to see?
questions.a: Mantle 2.9 cm, outer core 2.2 cm, inner core 1.25 cm, lithosphere 0.1 cm (1 mm). Continental crust 30 / 1000 = 0.03 cm, or 0.3 mm, so it would hardly be visible as a layer.
s: Mantle and core lengths: 2.9, 2.2 and 1.25 cm
Lithosphere 0.1 cm
Crust 0.03 cm, about 0.3 mm, so hardly visible

questions.q: Compare the crust, the mantle and the core as the chapter describes them. For each give its position and one feature, and then say which of them provides the plates with their upper surface and why the plates can move over what lies beneath.
questions.a: Crust: the outermost layer, on which we live; 30-40 km thick under continents and 5-7 km under oceans. Mantle: lies below the crust, very thick (about 2900 km) and hot; its upper part joins the crust to form the lithosphere. Core: the innermost layer, extremely hot and heavy; the outer core is fluid (iron and nickel) and the inner core is a solid, dense ball. The lithosphere, broken into plates, forms the upper surface; the plates move because below it lies the semi-molten asthenosphere.
s: Crust: position and thickness
Mantle: position and feature
Core: position, with inner and outer core contrasted
Lithosphere (crust + upper mantle) forms the plates
Plates move because of the semi-molten asthenosphere

questions.q: Explain how convection currents in the mantle move tectonic plates, and then work out how far a plate moving at 3 cm per year would travel in 50 lakh (5 million) years. Say what this shows about the speed of plate movement.
questions.a: Heat from the core makes molten mantle material rise while cooler material sinks. This continuous circulation creates convection currents which push and pull the plates in different directions. Distance = 3 cm x 5,000,000 = 15,000,000 cm = 150 km. Even though each year's movement is only a few centimetres, it adds up over millions of years to a very large distance.
s: Heat makes material rise and cooler material sink
Convection currents push and pull the plates
Calculation 3 x 5,000,000 cm
Answer 150 km
Conclusion: slow each year but large over millions of years

questions.q:
A geography club is building a model of the Earth for the school science fair. Its radius is 6375 km, and the club will use a scale of 1 cm to 500 km. The layers it needs to show are: lithosphere 100 km, asthenosphere 200 km, and the continental crust 30 km (which lies inside the lithosphere). Priya says the continental crust will be too thin to see, so she wants to draw it ten times thicker than the scale allows and write 'not to scale' under it. Karan wants every layer exactly to scale.
(a) What thickness in cm should the lithosphere ring have at this scale?
(b) Find the thickness of the asthenosphere ring in cm and name its nature.
(c) The continental crust, at scale, comes to 0.06 cm. Whose plan should the club follow? Choose and justify, saying what each plan gains and what it loses.
questions.a: (a) 100 / 500 = 0.2 cm. (b) 200 / 500 = 0.4 cm; the asthenosphere is a hot, mobile, semi-molten layer. (c) Either choice with the trade-off: Karan's plan is true to the proportions and shows how thin the crust really is (0.06 cm, about 0.6 mm), but visitors cannot see or label it. Priya's plan (0.6 cm) lets visitors see the crust and its position within the lithosphere, but a 'not to scale' label is needed or visitors will think it is thick.
s: (b) 0.4 cm; semi-molten and mobile
(c) Decision with a gain and a loss for each plan

questions.q:
Two survey markers, P and Q, are fixed on either side of a plate boundary and are found to be moving apart by 3 cm every year. A research institute has a measuring device accurate only to within 5 cm. Plan 1 monitors the markers for 3 years at a cost of Rs 4 lakh a year. Plan 2 monitors them for 10 years at the same yearly cost. The institute can afford only one plan.
(a) How far apart will the markers have moved after 3 years and after 10 years?
(b) Name the type of plate boundary where plates move apart and say what forms there.
(c) Which plan should the institute choose? Compare the movement with the device's accuracy and the total cost of each plan.
questions.a: (a) 3 x 3 = 9 cm after 3 years; 3 x 10 = 30 cm after 10 years. (b) A divergent boundary; magma rises from below and forms new crust, creating features such as mid-ocean ridges. (c) Plan 1 costs Rs 12 lakh but the 9 cm movement is only a little more than the 5 cm accuracy, so the result is doubtful. Plan 2 costs Rs 40 lakh, but 30 cm is six times the accuracy and gives a reliable result. Either choice is acceptable if the trade-off of cost against reliability is stated.
s: (a) 9 cm and 30 cm
(b) Divergent; new crust forms
(c) Cost Rs 12 lakh and Rs 40 lakh compared with 9 cm and 30 cm against a 5 cm accuracy, then a justified choice

questions.q: A geologist maps a long underwater ridge where hot magma is rising, cooling and adding new crust, while the plates on either side drift apart. Which type of plate boundary is this, and which feature in the chapter is its example?
questions.a: Divergent, as with the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Where plates move away from each other, magma rises and forms new crust, creating mid-ocean ridges such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. The San Andreas Fault is the chapter's example of a transform boundary.
o: Divergent, as with the Mid-Atlantic Ridge
Convergent, as with the Mid-Atlantic Ridge
Divergent, as with the San Andreas Fault
Transform, as with the San Andreas Fault

questions.q: An oceanic plate and a continental plate are pressed together. Which description fits what the chapter says happens?
questions.a: The oceanic plate sinks beneath the continental plate, causing volcanic activity and earthquakes. At a convergent boundary between an oceanic and a continental plate the oceanic plate sinks beneath, leading to volcanic activity and earthquakes. Fold mountains form when two continental plates collide.
o: The oceanic plate sinks beneath the continental plate, causing volcanic activity and earthquakes
Both plates are pushed upward and crumple into fold mountains such as the Himalaya
The plates slide past each other and no crust is formed or destroyed
The plates move apart and magma rises to form new crust between them

questions.q: A student places a map of the major plates beside a map of earthquakes and volcanoes. Which observation would best support the statement 'Plate movement explains where earthquakes and volcanoes occur'?
questions.a: Most earthquake and volcano points fall in belts along the edges of plates. The chapter says most earthquakes and volcanoes occur along plate boundaries, especially around the Pacific Ocean (the Ring of Fire); a pattern of belts along plate edges is what the theory predicts.
o: Most earthquake and volcano points fall in belts along the edges of plates
Earthquake and volcano points are spread evenly over every continent
Earthquake and volcano points lie only in the middle of the largest plates
Earthquake points are found, but volcano points appear only in deserts

questions.q: On a field trip to Baratang Island, Anita sees mud bubbling out of the ground. Her guide says it is India's only mud volcano. Which statement matches the chapter?
questions.a: The mud bubbles out because of natural underground gases and pressure, unlike a fiery volcano. The chapter says that at Baratang mud bubbles out due to natural underground gases and pressure, unlike fiery volcanoes.
o: The mud bubbles out because of natural underground gases and pressure, unlike a fiery volcano
The mud bubbles out because an oceanic plate is sinking beneath the island at that very spot
The mud is molten rock from the core, the same material that a fiery volcano throws out
The mud appears because plates slide past each other without making or destroying crust

questions.q:
Assertion (A): At a transform boundary the sliding plates destroy old crust.
Reason (R): Movement at a transform boundary mainly causes earthquakes, such as along the San Andreas Fault.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. A is false: at a transform boundary plates slide past each other without creating or destroying crust. R is a true statement from the chapter.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
Read the statements about plate boundaries.
1. At a divergent boundary the plates move towards each other, and this is how fold mountains such as the Himalaya form.
2. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is an example of a boundary where plates move away from each other and new crust forms.
3. When an oceanic plate collides with a continental plate, the oceanic plate sinks beneath it.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only. Statement 1 is false: plates move towards each other at a convergent boundary; at a divergent boundary they move apart. Statements 2 and 3 are from the chapter.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: On a map, earthquake points form a long narrow line along a fault where two plates slide past each other and no crust is made or destroyed. This is a ___ boundary.
questions.a: transform

questions.q: Which one of these pairs of events and boundaries is correctly matched according to the chapter?
questions.a: Fold mountains: collision of two continental plates. Fold mountains such as the Himalaya form where continental plates collide. The other pairings swap the boundary types.
o: Fold mountains: collision of two continental plates
Volcanoes alone: plates sliding past each other
New crust: oceanic plate sinking under a continental plate
Mid-ocean ridge: two continental plates colliding

questions.q: True or False: A transform boundary neither creates nor destroys crust, yet it can still be the scene of earthquakes.
questions.a: True. At a transform boundary plates slide past each other without creating or destroying crust, and this movement mainly causes earthquakes, as along the San Andreas Fault.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: plates slide past without making or destroying crust, and the sliding causes earthquakes

questions.q: (a) What happens to an oceanic plate when it collides with a continental plate? (b) Name the two kinds of event this can lead to.
questions.a: (a) The oceanic plate sinks beneath the continental plate. (b) Volcanic activity and earthquakes.
s: (a) Oceanic plate sinks beneath the continental plate
(b) Volcanic activity and earthquakes

questions.q: Differentiate between a convergent boundary and a divergent boundary by saying how the plates move and giving one example of a result of each.
questions.a: At a convergent boundary the plates move towards each other, e.g. continental plates colliding form fold mountains such as the Himalaya. At a divergent boundary they move away from each other, magma rises and forms new crust, e.g. the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
s: Convergent: plates move together, with a result
Divergent: plates move apart, with a result

questions.q: Why are most of the world's earthquakes and volcanoes found in a ring around the Pacific Ocean? Use the term used for this area.
questions.a: This area is called the Ring of Fire. Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur along plate boundaries, and this is especially so around the Pacific Ocean, so they cluster there.
s: Names the Ring of Fire
Links the quakes and volcanoes to plate boundaries

questions.q: (a) Name two of the four elemental forces to which Varahamihira attributed earthquakes in the Bṛihatsaṁhitā. (b) Which words in the chapter show that this was an early attempt to use observation and reasoning?
questions.a: (a) Any two of Vayu (wind), Agni (fire), Indra (heaven/thunder) and Varuna (water). (b) He noted how changes in wind, rain, clouds, animal behaviour and planetary alignments could signal earthquakes, so the book calls it an early attempt to blend observations with cosmological reasoning.
s: (a) Two of the four forces named correctly
(b) Observations of wind, rain, clouds or animals used as signs

questions.q: Isha says, 'When two continental plates collide they form fold mountains like the Himalaya, but when an oceanic plate meets a continental plate, the oceanic one sinks and this leads to volcanoes and earthquakes.' Is she right? Answer with the chapter.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. The chapter says continental plates colliding form fold mountains such as the Himalaya, while an oceanic plate colliding with a continental plate sinks beneath it, leading to volcanic activity and earthquakes. Both are convergent boundaries but they give different results.
s: Verdict: right
Continental collision: fold mountains such as the Himalaya
Oceanic-continental: oceanic plate sinks, volcanoes and earthquakes

questions.q: Show that a transform boundary cannot give rise to a mid-ocean ridge such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
questions.a: A mid-ocean ridge forms where plates move away from each other and magma rises to form new crust, which happens at a divergent boundary. At a transform boundary plates slide past each other without creating or destroying crust, so no new crust forms there and no ridge can be built.
s: Ridge needs plates moving apart and new crust (divergent)
Transform: plates slide past without creating crust
Conclusion that a ridge cannot form

questions.q: Name the boundary type, and one result, in each case: (i) magma rises between two plates moving apart; (ii) plates slide past each other along a fault; (iii) an oceanic plate sinks beneath a continental plate.
questions.a: (i) Divergent boundary; new crust (a mid-ocean ridge) forms. (ii) Transform boundary; earthquakes. (iii) Convergent boundary; volcanic activity and earthquakes.
s: (i) Divergent with new crust
(ii) Transform with earthquakes
(iii) Convergent with volcanoes and earthquakes

questions.q: Compare the three types of plate boundary. For each, state the movement of the plates, what happens to the crust, one example the chapter gives, and one hazard or feature it produces.
questions.a: Convergent: plates move towards each other; continental plates colliding fold up into mountains such as the Himalaya, and an oceanic plate sinks under a continental plate, causing volcanoes and earthquakes. Divergent: plates move away; magma rises and new crust forms, e.g. the Mid-Atlantic Ridge (a mid-ocean ridge). Transform: plates slide past each other without creating or destroying crust, e.g. the San Andreas Fault, mainly causing earthquakes.
s: Convergent: movement and crust result
Divergent: movement, new crust and example
Transform: movement, no crust change, example
Hazard or feature matched to each type

questions.q: 'Plate movements are responsible for the distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes.' Justify this statement using the Ring of Fire and one boundary type of your choice, and say why an earthquake in a densely populated country such as India can be especially serious.
questions.a: Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur along plate boundaries, and a map of the plates matches the map of earthquakes and volcanoes. This is especially so around the Pacific Ocean, an area known as the Ring of Fire. For example, where an oceanic plate sinks beneath a continental plate there is volcanic activity and earthquakes. India has had major earthquakes (such as Gujarat in 2001) in which thousands died; in a densely populated country a large earthquake can cause severe damage to life and the environment.
s: Most quakes and volcanoes lie along plate boundaries
Ring of Fire around the Pacific
A boundary type linked to a specific hazard
India has had major earthquakes with thousands of deaths
Dense population increases damage

questions.q:
A state disaster cell has money for monitoring stations in two of three towns. Town X lies where an oceanic plate is sinking beneath a continental plate, and has 40,000 people. Town Y lies on a fault where two plates slide past each other and has 8 lakh people. Town Z lies in the middle of a large plate, far from any plate boundary, with 2 lakh people.
(a) Name the hazard or hazards expected at X and at Y.
(b) Which town would the chapter's theory suggest is least likely to have earthquakes and volcanoes, and why?
(c) The cell can fund only two stations. Which two towns should it choose? Justify, using the hazards and the populations.
questions.a: (a) X: volcanic activity and earthquakes; Y: earthquakes. (b) Town Z, because most earthquakes and volcanoes occur along plate boundaries and Z is far from any boundary. (c) Either answer if justified. X and Y are the two sites with plate-boundary hazards; Y has by far the largest population (8 lakh) and X is exposed to two hazards though only 40,000 live there. Choosing X and Y covers both boundary hazards; choosing Y and Z would be hard to defend because Z is far from a boundary.
s: (a) X: volcanoes and earthquakes; Y: earthquakes
(b) Z, since it is far from any boundary
(c) A choice justified with hazards and populations

questions.q:
The Andaman and Nicobar tourism board is reviewing visits to the mud volcano at Baratang. At present 300 visitors come each day and pay Rs 150 each. The board is considering a cap of 200 visitors a day with the ticket raised to Rs 250. Some board members worry that a large crowd on the soft ground near bubbling mud is a risk; others say the cap would reduce local boatmen's earnings.
(a) Say how the Baratang mud volcano differs from a fiery volcano.
(b) What makes the mud bubble out, according to the chapter?
(c) Find the daily ticket income under each plan and decide which plan the board should adopt. State what each side gains and loses.
questions.a: (a) A fiery volcano erupts hot material; at Baratang mud bubbles out instead. (b) Natural underground gases and pressure. (c) Current plan: 300 x 150 = Rs 45,000 a day. Capped plan: 200 x 250 = Rs 50,000 a day, so ticket income rises by Rs 5,000 with fewer people on the site. But 100 fewer visitors a day may reduce boatmen's and shopkeepers' earnings. Either plan can be defended if this trade-off is stated.
s: (a) Mud rather than fiery eruption
(b) Underground gases and pressure
(c) Rs 45,000 and Rs 50,000 with a justified choice and trade-off

questions.q: A banyan seedling takes root in a crack of an old fort wall in Rajasthan, and years later the wall stone has split in two. Which type of weathering, according to the chapter, is at work?
questions.a: Biological weathering, caused by plant roots. The chapter gives plant roots growing into rock cracks and splitting them as its example of biological weathering.
o: Biological weathering, caused by plant roots
Physical weathering, caused by frost and wind
Chemical weathering, caused by acids in rain
Erosion, caused by wind carrying the stone away

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an example of erosion as the chapter defines it?
questions.a: Rock cracks on a hill and the pieces stay where they fall. Erosion involves the movement of the broken material by water, wind, ice or waves. Rock that breaks and stays in place is weathering, which does not involve movement.
o: Rock cracks on a hill and the pieces stay where they fall
Wind lifts loose sand from a dry area and drops it far away
Heavy rain washes the topsoil of a field into a nearby river
Sea waves wear away land along the shore

questions.q: Farmers on a hillside dig long trenches along the lines of equal height of the slope to slow down rainwater, hold it and let it soak in. Which conservation practice from the chapter is this?
questions.a: Contouring. The chapter describes a continuous contour trench dug along the contour lines to slow, hold and infiltrate rainwater and prevent erosion.
o: Contouring
Bunding
Terracing
Building check dams

questions.q: After every rainy season a farmer in a hilly area finds the dark top layer of her field thinner and her crop yield lower. Which process and effect from the chapter explain this?
questions.a: Erosion has carried off the topsoil, so yields fall. Erosion removes the fertile topsoil needed for crop growth, leading to lower yields. Weathering only breaks rock and does not carry material away.
o: Erosion has carried off the topsoil, so yields fall
Weathering has moved the fertile topsoil away, so yields fall
Deposition has added extra topsoil, so yields fall
Gradation has levelled the field, so yields rise

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Weathering and erosion are not the same process.
Reason (R): Weathering breaks rocks without moving the broken material, whereas erosion involves the movement of the broken material.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Both are true, and R is exactly the difference that makes A true.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. In chemical weathering the minerals in rocks change through reactions with water, air or acids and form new substances.
2. Erosion removes only solid rock; fertile soil is never carried away by it.
3. A check dam built across a small stream reduces the speed of water and lets sediment settle.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only. Statement 2 is false: erosion carries away soil and other surface materials too, which is why it removes fertile topsoil.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Match each conservation practice in Column I with what it does in Column II.
Column I: 1. Contouring  2. Bunding  3. Terracing  4. Check dams
Column II: (a) Level or gently sloping steps cut on a hillside  (b) Trenches dug along the contour lines of a hillside  (c) Earthen embankments along contour lines to slow run-off  (d) Structures across small streams that slow water and let sediment settle
questions.a: 1-b, 2-c, 3-a, 4-d. Contouring is the contour trench, bunding the earthen embankment, terracing the series of steps and check dams the structures across small streams.

questions.q: A village school in Nagaland studies the Zabo system of its state. Which description of it is correct?
questions.a: An integrated farming approach using earthen bunds on hillslopes to conserve soil and water. The chapter describes the Zabo system as an integrated farming approach using earthen bunds on hillslopes for soil and water conservation.
o: An integrated farming approach using earthen bunds on hillslopes to conserve soil and water
A system of level steps cut into a hillside for growing rice in standing water
A set of check dams that stops every stream from flowing down the hill slopes
A method of digging deep trenches along a river bank to prevent floods in the area

questions.q: True or False: Weathering and erosion are the same process, since in both of them broken rock is carried from one place to another.
questions.a: False. Weathering only breaks rocks down and does not involve movement of the broken material; erosion involves carrying the material away by water, wind, ice or waves.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: weathering has no movement of material, erosion does

questions.q: (a) Name the type of weathering in which the minerals in a rock change after reacting with rainwater, air or acids. (b) How does it differ from the weathering that splits a rock when frost freezes in its cracks?
questions.a: (a) Chemical weathering. (b) Chemical weathering changes the minerals into new substances, whereas frost (physical weathering) only breaks the rock into smaller pieces without changing what it is made of.
s: (a) Chemical weathering
(b) New substances formed, versus rock only broken into pieces by frost

questions.q: (a) Name two occupations that erosion affects, according to the chapter. (b) For one of them, explain what exactly is lost and how this reduces the worker's income.
questions.a: (a) Any two of farming, living near rivers or coasts, construction and mining, tourism and fishing. (b) E.g. a farmer loses the fertile topsoil, so crops grow poorly, yields fall and her income is lower; or a fisher or hotel owner loses beaches and rivers that attract fish or tourists.
s: (a) Two occupations named
(b) What is lost and the effect on earnings

questions.q: Differentiate between physical and biological weathering, giving one cause of each.
questions.a: Physical weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces because of temperature changes, frost or wind. Biological weathering is caused by plants, animals or micro-organisms, for example plant roots growing into cracks and splitting the rock.
s: Physical weathering with a cause (temperature change, frost or wind)
Biological weathering with a cause (plants, animals or micro-organisms)

questions.q: Which conservation practice does the Zabo system of Nagaland use? Explain in one line how this practice protects a hillside.
questions.a: It uses earthen bunds on hillslopes. Bunds are earthen embankments built along contour lines that slow surface run-off, reduce soil erosion and increase water infiltration and soil moisture.
s: Names the earthen bunds (bunding)
Slows run-off, reducing erosion and helping water soak in

questions.q: Kabir says, 'Erosion is always harmful; all it does is destroy the land.' How far is he right? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Not right. The chapter says erosion shapes landforms and can both create and destroy features on the Earth's surface. He is right that it can destroy, for example by washing away topsoil, houses and roads, but it also helps form features such as valleys, caves and river deltas.
s: Verdict: not right
The harmful side: topsoil, land and property lost
It also creates features, such as valleys and deltas

questions.q: Describe a place near your school or home where weathering is happening but erosion is not yet taking place. Say what you see, which type of weathering it is and why it is not yet erosion.
questions.a: Any valid example, e.g. a stone wall with cracks from heating by day and cooling by night: this is physical weathering, and since the broken bits stay on the wall or at its foot and are not being carried off by water, wind, ice or waves, it is not yet erosion.
s: A believable observed place and signs
The type of weathering named correctly
Reason: no movement of the broken material

questions.q: Using the chapter's links, explain in three steps how erosion on a hillside farm leads to a fall in the family's income, and name one practice that would break the chain.
questions.a: Erosion carries away the fertile topsoil, so crops grow poorly and yields are lower, and lower yields mean less produce to sell and a lower income. Terracing, contouring, bunding or check dams slow run-off and hold the soil, breaking the chain.
s: Erosion removes fertile topsoil
Lower yields then lower income
A named practice that holds the soil

questions.q: Name the five agents of gradation and, for each, describe one thing it does to the surface or one landform it makes, as the chapter says. Then explain in one sentence what 'gradation' achieves overall.
questions.a: Running water erodes rocks and soils to form valleys and plains. Glaciers scrape and carry material, carving U-shaped valleys. Wind shapes deserts by eroding and depositing sand. Sea waves erode coastlines to form cliffs, beaches and bays. Groundwater dissolves rocks such as limestone, creating caves and sinkholes. Together they wear down, transport and deposit material, lowering high areas and filling up low areas.
s: Running water and glaciers with their work
Wind and waves with their work
Groundwater with its work
All five agents named
Overall: lowers high areas and fills low ones

questions.q: The panchayat of a hill village wants a plan to protect its sloping fields from erosion. Choose any two of contouring, bunding, terracing and check dams, say how each works, and explain why each suits a hillside. Add one fact from the chapter showing that these practices are old.
questions.a: E.g. Terracing makes a series of level or gently sloping steps on the hillside so soil and water are held on each step. Bunding builds earthen embankments along contour lines, slowing run-off, reducing erosion and increasing soil moisture. Contouring digs trenches along contour lines and check dams slow streams and let sediment settle. These practices were used by the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation and are recorded in Sanskrit texts such as the Vedas and Kautilya's Arthashastra.
s: First practice and how it works
Second practice and how it works
Why each suits a slope (slows run-off and holds soil)
Sindhu-Sarasvati practice named as ancient
Source texts or an example such as Zabo

questions.q:
A hill village has 25 acres of sloping fields and Rs 6 lakh to protect them. Terracing costs Rs 18,000 per acre, bunding Rs 9,000 per acre, and each check dam on the stream above the fields costs Rs 1.5 lakh. The panchayat is choosing between Plan P: terracing all 25 acres plus one check dam, and Plan Q: bunding all 25 acres plus two check dams.
(a) Which practice makes a series of level or gently sloping steps on a hillside?
(b) What do check dams do to the speed of the stream and to the sediment it carries?
(c) Find the cost of each plan and decide which the panchayat should choose, naming one gain and one loss of your choice.
questions.a: (a) Terracing. (b) They reduce the speed of the water and let sediment settle, which also helps groundwater recharge. (c) Plan P: 25 x 18,000 = Rs 4.5 lakh + Rs 1.5 lakh = Rs 6 lakh (exactly the budget). Plan Q: 25 x 9,000 = Rs 2.25 lakh + 2 x 1.5 = Rs 3 lakh = Rs 5.25 lakh, leaving Rs 75,000. Either is acceptable if justified: P gives level steps over the whole field but only one stream check; Q holds the soil with cheaper bunds and slows the stream twice, with money left over, but gives no level steps.
s: (a) Terracing
(b) Slows water and lets sediment settle
(c) Costs Rs 6 lakh and Rs 5.25 lakh with a justified choice

questions.q:
Bankura, a village on a river bank, has 120 m of farmland between the river bank and the main road. Surveyors find that the river's bank loses 6 m of land every year. Moving the road inland would cost Rs 80 lakh. Building check dams on the small stream that feeds the river costs Rs 1.5 lakh each, and the panchayat could build four of them, but nobody can say how much they would slow the bank loss.
(a) In how many years will the bank reach the road at the present rate?
(b) Which of the village's property and activities does the chapter say are at risk when a river or coast erodes land?
(c) Should the panchayat move the road at once or try the check dams first? Weigh the cost against the certainty.
questions.a: (a) 120 / 6 = 20 years. (b) Land, houses and roads can be washed away, causing damage and loss of property (and farming loses fertile topsoil). (c) Either with reasons. Four check dams cost 4 x 1.5 = Rs 6 lakh, far less than Rs 80 lakh, and the chapter says check dams slow water and let sediment settle, but their effect on this bank is unknown; moving the road is certain but about 13 times as costly. With 20 years in hand, trying the check dams first and monitoring is defensible; moving at once is safer if the result is uncertain.
s: (a) 20 years
(b) Land, houses and roads, with loss of property
(c) Costs Rs 6 lakh and Rs 80 lakh weighed against certainty, with a justified choice

questions.q: Tourists watch a river drop over a vertical cliff in the hills. A guide says that hard rock lies on top and softer rock lies below. Which explanation from the chapter accounts for the sudden drop?
questions.a: The softer rock below is worn away faster, while the hard rock above resists erosion. A waterfall forms in the upper course where hard rocks resist erosion while softer rocks below are worn away, creating a sudden drop.
o: The softer rock below is worn away faster, while the hard rock above resists erosion
The hard rock above is worn away faster, while the softer rock below resists erosion
The river deposits sediment on the cliff and builds a step of rock
The river slows in the upper course and deposits large amounts of sediment

questions.q: Farmers want fresh fertile silt for their fields at a sharp bend in a river's middle course. On which part of the bend should they expect to find silt being deposited?
questions.a: The inner bank of the bend. At a meander the river erodes the outer bank and deposits sediment on the inner bank, which is why fertile soil builds up there.
o: The inner bank of the bend
The outer bank of the bend
The middle of the river bed in the upper course
The steep valley wall above the bend

questions.q: An agricultural officer must pick a site where rice and jute can grow on rich alluvial soil, where fishing is good because fresh water mixes with salt water, and where rivers give navigable routes. Which landform from the chapter fits best?
questions.a: A delta at the mouth of a river. Deltas are highly fertile, ideal for crops such as rice and jute, rich in aquatic life from the mix of fresh and salt water, and centres of trade because rivers provide navigable routes.
o: A delta at the mouth of a river
An oxbow lake in the middle course
A V-shaped valley in the upper course
A waterfall in the upper course

questions.q: Which of these landforms is NOT one that the chapter places in the upper course of a river?
questions.a: Oxbow lake. V-shaped valleys, waterfalls and rapids form in the upper course because of steep gradients and strong erosion. Oxbow lakes and floodplains belong to the middle course.
o: Oxbow lake
V-shaped valley
Waterfall
Rapids

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A delta is a landform formed at the mouth of a river, where it flows into a sea, ocean or lake.
Reason (R): A delta forms because the river erodes more strongly at its mouth than anywhere else along its course.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. A is true: the delta is built where the river deposits the sediments it has carried from upstream. R is false: it is deposition, not erosion, that builds a delta.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the courses of a river.
1. In the upper course steep gradients and strong erosion give V-shaped valleys, waterfalls and rapids.
2. In the middle course the river loses energy and begins depositing sediments, forming meanders, oxbow lakes and floodplains.
3. In the lower course the river slows further and deposits large amounts of sediment, forming deltas, levees and alluvial fans.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3. All three statements are from the chapter's description of the upper, middle and lower courses.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 only

questions.q: Along a bend of a river, the water cuts away the outer bank and leaves sediment on the ___ bank.
questions.a: inner

questions.q: A hill district wants a landform that can supply electricity from the force of falling water and also attract trekkers and photographers. Which landform from the chapter would the planners choose?
questions.a: A waterfall. The chapter says waterfalls are sometimes used for hydroelectric power, as the force of the falling water can be harnessed, and give opportunities for trekking and photography.
o: A waterfall
A delta
A meander
A floodplain

questions.q: True or False: Deltas form in the steep upper course of a river, where the water flows fastest and erodes most strongly.
questions.a: False. A delta forms at the mouth of the river, where it flows into a sea, ocean or lake and deposits the sediments carried from upstream. Strong erosion in the steep upper course gives V-shaped valleys and waterfalls instead.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: deltas form at the river mouth by deposition, not in the upper course

questions.q: (a) On a meander, which bank does the river erode and which does it build up with sediment? (b) Use your answer to explain why the loops of a meander gradually grow larger.
questions.a: (a) It erodes the outer bank and deposits sediment on the inner bank. (b) Because the outer bank is cut back while the inner bank is built up, each bend moves outward and the loops grow larger.
s: (a) Erodes the outer bank and deposits on the inner bank
(b) Outer bank retreats while inner bank grows, so the loop enlarges

questions.q: Differentiate between the work of a river in its upper course and in its lower course, giving one landform of each.
questions.a: In the upper course the gradient is steep and erosion is strong, giving landforms such as V-shaped valleys, waterfalls and rapids. In the lower course the river slows and deposits large amounts of sediment, giving landforms such as deltas, levees and alluvial fans.
s: Upper course: strong erosion, with a landform
Lower course: deposition, with a landform

questions.q: (a) Name two crops that deltas support. (b) Deltas are prone to flooding, yet many carry dense human settlements. Give two reasons from the chapter why people still live there.
questions.a: (a) Rice and jute. (b) Any two of: highly fertile alluvial soil suits farming; fishing is good because of the mix of fresh and salt water; they are centres of trade and transport since rivers give navigable routes.
s: (a) Rice and jute
(b) Two reasons for settlement

questions.q: Where does the Grand Anicut (Kallanai) in Tamil Nadu fit into the chapter's discussion, and what does it show about how humans use rivers?
questions.a: It is the chapter's example in the discussion of meanders of the use of a river for irrigation, showing that people harness rivers to water their fields.
s: Names it as an example of using a river
Says the use is irrigation

questions.q: Nisha says, 'A river erodes most in its lower course, where it carries the most sediment, and deposits most in its upper course.' Is she right? Answer using the chapter.
questions.a: No, she has it the wrong way round. In the upper course the steep gradient and strong erosive force erode the land (V-shaped valleys, waterfalls). In the lower course the river slows and deposits large amounts of sediment, forming deltas, levees and alluvial fans.
s: Verdict: not right
Upper course: strong erosion
Lower course: deposition of sediment

questions.q: Show that a delta could not form in the steep upper course of a river.
questions.a: A delta is formed at the river's mouth, where the river flows into a sea, ocean or lake and deposits the sediments it has carried from upstream. In the upper course the river is steep and its erosive force is strong, so it cuts valleys rather than depositing the load of sediment that builds a delta.
s: A delta needs deposition of carried sediment
Upper course is steep with strong erosion, not deposition
Conclusion: the deposition that builds a delta is missing upstream

questions.q: Write a short account of a river's journey from the hills to the sea, naming one landform in each of its three courses.
questions.a: E.g. The river begins in the hills in its upper course, cutting a V-shaped valley and dropping as a waterfall. In the middle course it loses energy and winds in a meander, leaving an oxbow lake and a floodplain. In the lower course it slows, forms levees and finally spreads into a delta where it meets the sea.
s: Upper course landform (V-shaped valley, waterfall or rapids)
Middle course landform (meander, oxbow lake or floodplain)
Lower course landform (delta, levee or alluvial fan) and the sea at the end

questions.q: Describe how the work of a river changes from its upper course to its lower course. For each of the three courses, name the main process and two landforms, and for one landform explain how it helps people.
questions.a: Upper course: steep gradient and strong erosion give V-shaped valleys, waterfalls and rapids. Middle course: the river loses energy, begins depositing sediments and meanders; oxbow lakes and floodplains form. Lower course: the river slows further and deposits large amounts of sediment, forming deltas, levees and alluvial fans. Use, e.g. waterfalls give hydroelectric power and tourism, or deltas give fertile land for rice and jute.
s: Upper course: process and landforms
Middle course: process and landforms
Lower course: process and landforms
A landform's use to people
The overall change from erosion to deposition

questions.q: A state government is deciding whether to build a new port town in a river delta. List two advantages and two risks that the chapter gives for deltas, and say what you would advise, justifying your advice.
questions.a: Advantages: fertile alluvial soil for crops such as rice and jute; good fishing; dense settlement; centres of trade and transport because rivers give navigable routes. Risks: deltas are prone to flooding that affects human life and activities. Advice: either, if justified, e.g. build the port because the delta gives trade routes and food, but plan for floods; or choose a site away from the delta because flooding affects life and activity.
s: Two advantages from the chapter
Flood risk from the chapter
A second risk or limit stated
A clear recommendation
A justification that weighs the advantages against the risk

questions.q:
A family farms 10 acres in a river delta. A rice crop earns Rs 30,000 per acre in a normal year and nothing in a flood year. Fish ponds on the same land earn Rs 40,000 per acre in a normal year, but in a flood year they lose Rs 10,000 per acre. Floods have struck once in every 5 years. The family has farmed only rice so far.
(a) Why is delta soil especially good for rice?
(b) What feature of the water in a delta helps fishing?
(c) Work out the average yearly income per acre of each choice over a 5-year cycle, and advise the family: should it shift all its land to fish, keep rice, or divide it? Give reasons.
questions.a: (a) The soil is rich alluvial soil deposited by the river. (b) The mix of fresh water and salt water creates diverse aquatic life. (c) Rice: 4 normal years x 30,000 = 1,20,000 per 5 years, i.e. Rs 24,000 a year. Fish: 4 x 40,000 - 10,000 = 1,50,000 per 5 years, i.e. Rs 30,000 a year. Fish pays Rs 6,000 more per acre per year (Rs 60,000 a year over 10 acres), but the family has no experience of fish farming and loses money in a flood year; rice has no loss in a flood. Any of the three choices is acceptable if justified by this trade-off.
s: (a) Rich alluvial soil
(b) Mix of fresh and salt water
(c) Rs 24,000 and Rs 30,000 with a justified recommendation

questions.q:
A waterfall in a hill district draws 2,00,000 visitors a year, each paying Rs 120. A power company offers to build a hydroelectric station that would pay the district Rs 3 crore a year, but it would divert much of the water and the district expects visits to fall by half. The waterfall also has cultural and religious significance, and local families earn from trekking and photography guiding.
(a) Which kind of rock above and below the drop explains how this waterfall formed?
(b) Besides tourism, name two uses or values of waterfalls that the chapter mentions.
(c) Work out the district's yearly income from each option and decide which it should accept, saying what is gained and what is lost.
questions.a: (a) Hard rock above resists erosion while the softer rock below is worn away. (b) Any two of hydroelectric power, recreation such as trekking and photography, cultural or religious significance. (c) Now: 2,00,000 x 120 = Rs 2.4 crore. With the station: Rs 3 crore + (1,00,000 x 120 = Rs 1.2 crore) = Rs 4.2 crore, Rs 1.8 crore more. But the diverted water would reduce the fall's beauty and the religious and guiding value; either choice is acceptable if the cash gain is weighed against these losses.
s: (a) Hard rock resisting, softer rock worn away
(b) Two uses or values
(c) Rs 2.4 crore and Rs 4.2 crore with a justified decision

questions.q: On a rocky coast a boatman says that last monsoon the roof of a rock arch fell into the sea, and now only an isolated pillar of rock stands offshore. What is the pillar called, and how did the arch it came from form?
questions.a: A sea stack; the arch formed when caves on opposite sides of a headland met. Stacks are isolated pillars of rock left standing after arches collapse, and arches are created when caves on opposite sides of a headland meet.
o: A sea stack; the arch formed when caves on opposite sides of a headland met
A sea stack; the arch formed when sand was deposited across a bay
A wave-cut platform; the arch formed when caves on opposite sides of a headland met
A sea cliff; the arch formed when waves undercut the base of the coast

questions.q: A trekker in the mountains sees a bowl-shaped hollow at the head of a glacier and, between two neighbouring valleys, a sharp ridge. Which pair of terms from the chapter names these two features, in that order?
questions.a: Cirque and arete. A cirque is a bowl-shaped depression at the head of a glacier and an arete is a sharp ridge between valleys; the pair in the reverse order would name them the wrong way round.
o: Cirque and arete
Arete and cirque
Fjord and moraine
Hanging valley and till

questions.q: A tourist in a desert sees a sand dune with several arms, in a place where the wind blows from different directions at different times. Which type of dune is it?
questions.a: A star dune. Star dunes have multiple arms and form where winds come from different directions. Barchans are crescent-shaped with a single wind direction, longitudinal dunes lie parallel to the prevailing wind, and parabolic dunes are U-shaped and stabilised by vegetation.
o: A star dune
A barchan dune
A longitudinal dune
A parabolic dune

questions.q: In a limestone region, a farmer finds that the ground in one corner of her field has suddenly collapsed into a deep hole, and her neighbour reports an underground stream below a cave nearby. Which landform from the chapter explains the hole, and what made it?
questions.a: A sinkhole, formed when the ground collapses into a cavity that acidic water has dissolved. Sinkholes (dolines) are depressions formed when the ground collapses into an underground cavity, in areas where acidic water dissolves soluble rock such as limestone.
o: A sinkhole, formed when the ground collapses into a cavity that acidic water has dissolved
A cirque, formed when a small glacier hollows out the head of a valley
A deflation hollow, formed when wind removes loose material from the surface
A stalagmite, formed when dripping water builds a formation rising from the floor

questions.q:
Assertion (A): U-shaped valleys and cirques often attract trekkers and skiers.
Reason (R): Glaciers are a crucial source of fresh water, feeding rivers that sustain populations downstream.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Both statements are true, but the water supply role of glaciers does not explain why trekkers and skiers are drawn to those landforms.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements about landforms.
1. A sea arch forms after a sea stack has been worn down by waves.
2. Longitudinal dunes are long ridges formed at right angles to the prevailing wind.
3. Stalactites hang from the ceilings of caves, while stalagmites rise from their floors.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 3 only. Statement 1 is false: a stack is left after an arch collapses. Statement 2 is false: longitudinal dunes lie parallel to the prevailing wind. Statement 3 is correct.
o: 3 only
1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Match each glacial landform in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Cirque  2. Arete  3. Hanging valley  4. Fjord
Column II: (a) Sharp ridge between valleys  (b) Bowl-shaped depression at the head of a glacier  (c) Occurs where smaller glaciers meet larger ones  (d) Deep, narrow inlet made when the sea floods a glacial valley
questions.a: 1-b, 2-a, 3-c, 4-d. The cirque is the bowl at the glacier's head, the arete the sharp ridge, the hanging valley is where smaller glaciers meet larger ones and the fjord is the inlet made when the sea floods a glacial valley.

questions.q: A ridge of till lies across a valley at the very end of a glacier, marking the farthest point the glacier reached. It is called a ___ moraine.
questions.a: terminal

questions.q: True or False: A sea arch and the sea stack that follows it can both be made by waves on the same headland.
questions.a: True. Arches are created when caves on opposite sides of a headland meet; when an arch collapses, the isolated pillar of rock left standing is a stack. Both are products of wave erosion.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: caves meet to make an arch, and the collapsed arch leaves a stack

questions.q: (a) What is the debris that a glacier carries and leaves behind called? (b) Which type of moraine forms where two glaciers meet and their lateral moraines join, and where does it lie?
questions.a: (a) Till. (b) A medial moraine, formed in the middle when two glaciers meet and their lateral moraines join.
s: (a) Till
(b) Medial moraine, in the middle where lateral moraines join

questions.q: Differentiate between a stalactite and a stalagmite, saying where each is found in a cave.
questions.a: A stalactite is an icicle-shaped formation hanging from the ceiling of a cave; a stalagmite is a formation rising from the floor of a cave.
s: Stalactite hangs from the ceiling
Stalagmite rises from the floor

questions.q: (a) Which wind landform is a flat surface left behind after finer particles are blown away? (b) How is it different from a deflation hollow, which is also made by wind?
questions.a: (a) A desert pavement. (b) A deflation hollow (blowout) is a shallow depression formed where loose material is removed, while a desert pavement is the flat surface that remains after the finer particles have gone.
s: (a) Desert pavement
(b) Deflation hollow is a depression; pavement is a flat surface left behind

questions.q: Give two ways in which beaches help the people of a coastal village, according to the chapter.
questions.a: Any two of: tourism (relaxation, swimming, recreation) that boosts the local economy; fishing areas; collecting sand and shells; acting as natural barriers against strong waves and coastal erosion that safeguard settlements.
s: First valid use
Second valid use

questions.q: Rina says, 'All coastal landforms are made by waves depositing material, so waves only build land and never wear it away.' How far is she right?
questions.a: Partly right. Beaches and sand bars are made by deposition, so waves do build land. But she is wrong to say waves never wear land away: coastal erosion produces cliffs, wave-cut platforms, caves, arches and stacks.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right half: beaches or sand bars come from deposition
Wrong half: cliffs, caves, arches and stacks come from erosion

questions.q: Show that a sea stack cannot exist before a sea arch has formed on the same headland.
questions.a: Stacks are isolated pillars of rock left standing after the arches collapse. An arch itself is created when caves on opposite sides of a headland meet. So the order is cave, arch, stack; a stack is what remains of an arch, so it cannot appear first.
s: A stack is left standing after an arch collapses
An arch forms when caves on opposite sides of a headland meet
Conclusion about the order

questions.q: State three ways in which sand dunes are useful to people, as the chapter says.
questions.a: Any three of: they act as natural barriers against desertification and wind erosion; they provide areas for tourism and adventure sports; in some coastal regions they protect settlements from strong sea winds and waves; their sand is sometimes used for construction.
s: First use
Second use
Third use

questions.q: Compare how sea waves and glaciers shape the land. Name two landforms made by each, say how each is formed, and give one way in which humans use a landform of each.
questions.a: Waves: cliffs are steep rock faces formed as waves undercut the base of the coast; caves form where waves erode weak parts of rock; arches and stacks follow. Beaches are used for tourism, fishing and as natural barriers. Glaciers: U-shaped valleys are formed as glaciers widen and deepen river valleys; cirques are bowl-shaped depressions at the head of a glacier. U-shaped valleys and cirques are used for trekking, skiing and mountaineering, and fjords as harbours.
s: Two wave landforms named
How each wave landform forms
Two glacial landforms named with their formation
A human use of a wave landform
A human use of a glacial landform

questions.q: Explain how water makes caves, stalactites, stalagmites and sinkholes in areas of limestone. Then say what value these landforms have for people, and why the chapter calls the whole region Karst topography.
questions.a: In limestone or other soluble rocks, acidic underground water dissolves the rock by chemical weathering and erosion, forming caves. Stalactites hang from the cave ceiling, stalagmites rise from the floor, and sinkholes form when the ground collapses into an underground cavity. Underground rivers flow through cave systems. These give fresh water, tourism, cultural or religious importance and interest for geologists and adventurers. The set of landforms created in this way is called Karst topography.
s: Acidic water dissolves soluble rock to make caves
Stalactites and stalagmites placed correctly
Sinkholes form by collapse into a cavity
Values: fresh water, tourism, religious or cultural significance
Term Karst topography

questions.q:
A coastal village has a beach that protects its houses from strong waves. Forty families earn Rs 6,000 a month each by collecting and selling sand and shells from it. An engineer estimates that if collection continues, the beach will thin and storms will cause damage worth Rs 15 lakh a year; if collection is banned, expected damage is Rs 3 lakh a year. The panchayat is considering a full ban.
(a) How is a beach formed, according to the chapter?
(b) Give the way in which the beach safeguards the settlement.
(c) Work out the families' yearly earnings from collection and the yearly damage saved by a ban, and advise the panchayat on a full ban, a partial limit or no ban.
questions.a: (a) By the deposition of sediments (sand, pebbles or rocks) by waves. (b) It acts as a natural barrier against strong waves and coastal erosion. (c) Earnings: 40 x 6,000 x 12 = Rs 28.8 lakh a year. Damage saved by a ban: 15 - 3 = Rs 12 lakh a year. A full ban protects the houses but costs families more than twice what it saves in damage; no ban risks the houses; a partial limit is a middle course. Any choice is acceptable if the numbers and the protection role are weighed.
s: (a) Deposition by waves
(b) Natural barrier against waves and erosion
(c) Rs 28.8 lakh and Rs 12 lakh, with a justified recommendation

questions.q:
A panchayat in a limestone region wants to build a school for 300 students. Plot A lies near several sinkholes; its land costs Rs 40 lakh and surveying and filling will cost Rs 18 lakh more. Plot B is 2 km farther from the village; its land costs Rs 65 lakh, no collapse features are visible, and a school bus will cost Rs 4 lakh a year to run. The panchayat plans for a 10-year horizon.
(a) What is a sinkhole?
(b) What does a sinkhole near Plot A suggest about the ground beneath it?
(c) Find the 10-year cost of each plot and decide which the panchayat should choose, giving reasons that go beyond cost.
questions.a: (a) A depression formed when the ground collapses into an underground cavity. (b) That there may be cavities under the ground (soluble rock dissolved by acidic water), which can collapse. (c) Plot A: 40 + 18 = Rs 58 lakh. Plot B: 65 + 4 x 10 = Rs 105 lakh, Rs 47 lakh more. Plot A is much cheaper but sits above ground known to collapse into cavities, so safety of 300 students may outweigh cost; Plot B costs more but avoids the known hazard. Either decision is acceptable if safety and the Rs 47 lakh gap are both weighed.
s: (a) Ground collapses into an underground cavity
(b) Possible cavities beneath, from dissolved rock
(c) Rs 58 lakh and Rs 105 lakh with a justified decision

questions.q: After four days of continuous rain, a hillside above a village slips down. A student says rain alone cannot move soil. Which explanation from the chapter shows why heavy and continuous rain can trigger a landslide?
questions.a: Water seeps into the soil and rocks, increasing their weight and reducing friction. Heavy and continuous rainfall makes water seep into the soil and rocks, increasing their weight and reducing friction, so the slope can fail.
o: Water seeps into the soil and rocks, increasing their weight and reducing friction
Water seeps into the soil and rocks, decreasing their weight and increasing friction
Water freezes in the soil, raising the slope and making the ground steeper
Water dries the soil, so that strong winds can lift it off the slope

questions.q: On a mountain slope, a ski instructor notices that after a warm afternoon the snow has partly melted, and the layers no longer hold together. Which cause of avalanches from the chapter is this?
questions.a: A sudden rise in temperature partly melting the snow and reducing friction. A sudden rise in temperature can partially melt the snow and reduce the friction that holds it together.
o: A sudden rise in temperature partly melting the snow and reducing friction
Heavy snowfall within a short period adding extra weight to the snowpack
Strong winds piling up the snow unevenly into weak and fragile layers
Earthquakes and vibrations disturbing the balance of the snow-covered slope

questions.q: A glacial lake is held back by a wall of loose moraine. Over a hot summer the glacier melts rapidly, and then an avalanche falls into the lake. What does the chapter say can follow?
questions.a: The dam may collapse and suddenly release its water, flooding places downstream. Rapid melting raises the lake's size and water level and puts pressure on its natural dam; an avalanche striking the lake or weakening the dam can cause it to collapse and release the water abruptly, causing a Glacial Lake Outburst Flood.
o: The dam may collapse and suddenly release its water, flooding places downstream
The lake will freeze again and its dam will grow stronger from the added ice
The lake will dry up slowly, leaving a dust storm over the valley below
The water will be absorbed by the slope, causing a landslide upstream of the lake

questions.q: Which of these is NOT given in the chapter as a cause of dust storms?
questions.a: Heavy and continuous rainfall. Dust storms follow prolonged drought and low rainfall, sparse vegetation (deforestation, overgrazing, poor farming) and strong winds; heavy rainfall is a listed cause of landslides and GLOFs, not dust storms.
o: Heavy and continuous rainfall
Prolonged drought and low rainfall
Overgrazing that strips the vegetation cover
Strong winds lifting loose, dry soil

questions.q: A hill town wants to lower its landslide risk by acting on causes the chapter lists. Which step addresses a listed human cause?
questions.a: Improve drainage and end unplanned building on slopes. The chapter lists unplanned construction on hillsides and poor drainage as human factors in landslides; good drainage stops excess water from accumulating.
o: Improve drainage and end unplanned building on slopes
Plant crops with shallow roots on the steepest slope
Allow mining on the slope because it removes loose rocks
Build more roads cut into the hillside to ease the traffic

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Deforestation can increase the risk of landslides.
Reason (R): Deforestation, mining, road construction and unplanned building disturb the natural balance of slopes.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Both statements are true: the chapter lists deforestation among human activities that disturb the natural balance of slopes, which is why it raises the landslide risk.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements about landform-related disasters.
1. Poor drainage and improper land use can cause landslides by letting excess water accumulate.
2. A Glacial Lake Outburst Flood is caused only by a sudden fall in temperature that freezes the lake.
3. Dust storms are most likely where the land is thickly covered with vegetation.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only. Statement 2 is false: rapid melting from rising temperatures, heavy rain or snow, and earthquakes, avalanches or landslides can all cause GLOFs. Statement 3 is false: sparse vegetation leaves the land exposed to dust storms.
o: 1 only
2 only
1 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q: A glacial lake in a high valley is held back by a natural dam of ice or loose ___.
questions.a: moraine

questions.q: True or False: An earthquake can set off a landslide and can also lead to the collapse of the dam of a glacial lake.
questions.a: True. The chapter says earthquakes and volcanic eruptions can trigger landslides by shaking and weakening slopes, and that earthquakes, avalanches or landslides may strike a glacial lake or weaken its dam, leading to its collapse.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: earthquakes trigger landslides and can weaken a glacial lake's dam

questions.q: (a) Name two natural causes of landslides. (b) Explain how one of them makes a slope fail.
questions.a: (a) Any two of heavy and continuous rainfall, earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, steep slopes, loose or weathered rocks. (b) E.g. rain seeps in and adds weight while reducing friction; or earthquakes shake the ground and weaken the slopes.
s: (a) Two natural causes
(b) How one of them leads to slope failure

questions.q: (a) Name two human activities that can trigger an avalanche. (b) Why do such activities have this effect?
questions.a: (a) Any two of skiing, trekking, construction in mountainous areas. (b) They disturb the balance of snow-covered slopes.
s: (a) Two human activities
(b) They disturb the balance of the snow-covered slope

questions.q: Differentiate between a landslide and an avalanche by saying what is unstable on the slope in each, and giving one trigger common to both.
questions.a: In a landslide the soil and rocks of the slope fail; in an avalanche it is the snow on a steep mountain slope that becomes unstable. Earthquakes (or vibrations) can trigger both.
s: Landslide: soil and rock; avalanche: snow
A trigger common to both, such as earthquakes

questions.q: Why does the rapid melting of glaciers make a glacial lake more dangerous? Link the lake's water level to its natural dam.
questions.a: Rapid melting because of rising temperatures increases the size and water level of the glacial lake. This puts pressure on its natural dam of ice or loose moraine, making a sudden collapse and flood more likely.
s: Melting raises the lake's size and water level
Greater pressure on the ice or moraine dam

questions.q: Pooja says, 'Dust storms have natural causes, like drought and strong winds, and human causes too, like overgrazing and poor farming.' Is she right? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. Natural causes in the chapter are prolonged drought and low rainfall, strong winds lifting loose dry soil, and climate change or extreme weather; human causes include deforestation, overgrazing and poor farming practices that leave sparse vegetation and the land exposed.
s: Verdict: right
Natural causes named
Human causes named

questions.q: Show that a Glacial Lake Outburst Flood cannot take place in a region that has no glaciers and no glacial lakes.
questions.a: A GLOF is the sudden release of large volumes of water from a glacial lake, which is held by a natural dam of ice or loose moraine and fed by glacier melt. Without glaciers there is no melt water and no glacial lake, so there is no stored water or dam to fail, and no GLOF can occur.
s: A GLOF is a sudden release from a glacial lake
It depends on a glacial lake and its natural dam
No glacier, no lake, so no GLOF

questions.q: Write a short news report (3 or 4 lines) on a landslide on a hill road, naming two causes from the chapter that the reporter finds.
questions.a: Any valid report naming two listed causes, e.g. 'A stretch of the hill road slid after four days of heavy rain. Officials found that trees on the slope had been cleared and that the road drain was blocked, so water had collected behind the slope.'
s: A believable report of the event
First valid cause
Second valid cause

questions.q: Compare the causes of landslides, avalanches, GLOFs and dust storms. For each, name one natural cause and one human or climate-related cause the chapter gives.
questions.a: Landslides: natural, heavy rain or earthquakes; human, deforestation, mining or unplanned construction. Avalanches: natural, heavy snowfall or sudden rise in temperature; human, skiing, trekking or construction. GLOFs: natural, rapid melting of glaciers or heavy rain or earthquakes; the chapter links the melting to rising temperatures. Dust storms: natural, prolonged drought and strong winds; human, deforestation, overgrazing and poor farming, with climate change increasing frequency.
s: Landslides: a natural and a human cause
Avalanches: a natural and a human cause
GLOFs: causes
Dust storms: a natural and a human cause
Accurate comparison across the four, naming at least one cause common to two

questions.q: A hill village with a glacial lake above it, steep slopes, and a road under construction wants a risk plan. Using only the causes given in the chapter, list three actions the village could take or demand, say which disaster each lowers, and name one cause that the village cannot remove.
questions.a: E.g. (1) Stop unplanned construction and improve drainage on the slopes, lowering the landslide risk. (2) Limit trekking and construction on snow-covered slopes in avalanche season, lowering avalanche risk. (3) Watch the lake level and the condition of its moraine or ice dam, because rapid melting and heavy rain raise the GLOF risk. Causes the village cannot remove: earthquakes, heavy rainfall or rising temperatures.
s: First action linked to a listed cause and disaster
Second action linked to a listed cause and disaster
Third action linked to a listed cause and disaster
An uncontrollable natural cause named
Actions are matched correctly to the chapter's causes

questions.q:
A hill district must build an 18 km road to a remote village. Plan 1 cuts straight across steep slopes with loose rock and costs Rs 12 crore; it needs trees to be cleared on the slopes. Plan 2 follows gentler ground with proper drainage; it is 26 km long, costs Rs 17 crore and adds about 20 minutes to each trip. Villagers want the shorter road; the engineer worries about slope failure after heavy rain.
(a) Name two features of Plan 1 that the chapter lists as raising the landslide risk.
(b) Which feature of Plan 2 deals with a cause the chapter lists?
(c) Find the extra cost of Plan 2 and its cost per km compared with Plan 1, and decide which plan to build.
questions.a: (a) Steep slopes with loose rock, and clearing trees (deforestation). (b) Proper drainage, because poor drainage lets excess water collect and cause slope failure. (c) Extra cost: 17 - 12 = Rs 5 crore. Per km: Plan 1 12/18 = Rs 0.67 crore; Plan 2 17/26 = Rs 0.65 crore, so Plan 2 costs no more per km. Either decision is acceptable if justified: Plan 2 costs Rs 5 crore more and takes 20 minutes longer but avoids the steep, deforested slope; Plan 1 is quicker and cheaper in total but carries a higher landslide risk.
s: (a) Steep loose-rock slopes and tree clearing
(b) Proper drainage
(c) Rs 5 crore, Rs 0.67 and Rs 0.65 crore per km, with a justified decision

questions.q:
A village of 120 families lies 14 km downstream of a glacial lake held back by a wall of loose moraine. Over ten years the lake has grown as the glacier melts. The district can pay for only one measure: Plan 1, an early-warning system costing Rs 2.5 crore; or Plan 2, moving all 120 families to safer ground at Rs 8 lakh per family.
(a) What does 'GLOF' stand for?
(b) Give two events, other than rapid melting, that the chapter says can lead to the collapse of such a dam.
(c) Find the cost of Plan 2 and decide which plan the district should choose. Explain what each plan protects and what it leaves exposed.
questions.a: (a) Glacial Lake Outburst Flood. (b) Any two of heavy rainfall or intense snowfall adding water, earthquakes, avalanches or landslides striking the lake or weakening the dam. (c) Plan 2: 120 x 8 lakh = Rs 9.6 crore, Rs 7.1 crore more than Plan 1. Plan 1 gives warning time but families, homes and fields remain in the flood path; Plan 2 removes people from the path but costs far more and moves them from their land. Either choice is acceptable if both costs and safety are weighed.
s: (a) Glacial Lake Outburst Flood
(b) Two other causes
(c) Rs 9.6 crore and Rs 2.5 crore with a justified decision
